title: Pt-supported on N-doped carbon/TiO2 nanomaterials derived from NH2-MIL-125 for efficient photo-thermal RWGS reaction
journalName: Journal of Colloid and Interface Science
abstract:
To mitigate carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and advance carbon neutrality, the conversion of CO2 into value-added fuels and chemicals via the reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction is recognized as a promising approach. In this study, we designed platinum (Pt)-loaded nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanomaterials to achieve efficient photo-thermal performance in the RWGS reaction. The incorporation of Pt, nitrogen doping, and the selection of an appropriate calcination temperature enhance light responsiveness and reduce the recombination of photo-generated carriers, thereby improving the efficiency of the photo-thermal RWGS reaction. The optimized catalysts exhibited a high CO2 conversion (42.79 %), a carbon monoxide (CO) production rate (81.46 mmol gcat
                     −1 h−1) and over 99.9 % selectivity under conditions of 400 °C and 1.2 W cm−2 light illumination. In addition, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses revealed that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 was enriched with more oxygen defects, which was facilitate the adsorption and activation of CO2. CO temperature-programmed desorption (CO-TPD) showed that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 possesses a strong desorption capacity for CO. In addition, in-situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) pointed to COOH* as a key intermediate in the reaction process. The photo-thermal co-catalyzed CO2 reduction by CO-TPD as well as in-situ DRIFTS indicated that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 follows the RWGS reaction. This work provides a potential strategy for the synthesis of catalysts for enhancing photo-thermal co-catalyzed RWGS reactions.
paragraphs: No data was used for the research described in the article.

The emission of fossil fuels, especially carbon dioxide (CO2), has caused a series of environmental problems such as rising global temperatures, ocean acidification, and climate change. Therefore, there is an urgent need to strictly control and reduce this emission. In order to reduce CO2 emissions and favor carbon neutrality, converting CO2 into fuels and chemicals with the help of catalysts is considered a promising strategy. Reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) provides an opportunity to solve this problem. Since carbon monoxide (CO) is an important chemical raw material for the synthesis of fine chemicals and fuels, converting CO2 into CO through the RWGS reaction can obviously bring considerable economic benefits. However, the thermal-catalyzed RWGS reaction process consumes a lot of energy and has harsh reaction conditions, making it unsuitable for selective production. Most semiconductors in the photocatalyzed RWGS reaction have the characteristics of high recombination rate of photo-generated electron-hole pairs, limited absorption range, and low sunlight utilization rate. Therefore, an effective combination of thermal and photocatalysis was developed to improve high-performance catalysts and reaction processes [9,20–25].

Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is one of the most widely studied and promising photo-thermal catalysts due to its excellent properties such as chemical stability, environmental friendliness and low cost. However, TiO2 has a wide band gap, and the rapid recombination of electron-hole pairs results in poor response to visible light and a low catalytic reaction rate. Studies have shown that the appropriate arrangement of anatase and rutile phases to form a TiO2 phase junction not only accelerates charge transfer but also reduces the possibility of recombination of electron-hole pairs, thereby improving photo-thermal catalytic performance. In addition, the interface contacted between graphitic carbon and TiO2 is weak and the electron transfer distance is long, resulting in certain limitations on the separation of electron-hole pairs. Nitrogen-doped carbon can improve the response to light and reduce the recombination of photo-generated carriers. For example, Liu et al., successfully synthesized N-doped mesoporous carbon encapsulated anatase–rutile phase junction TiO2 (TiO2@CN), which exhibited very high photo-catalytic efficiency and mineralization efficiency. So far, TiO2 supported metals catalysts have made great progress in RWGS reactions. For example, Tang et al., synthesized an efficient catalyst composed of Rh nanoparticles supported on TiO2 nanosheets for light-assisted thermal catalytic CO2 hydrogenation. The catalyst has a CO yield of up to 20.6 mmol gcat −1 h−1 and a selectivity of 100 %. However, the most of TiO2 supported metal-based catalysts currently studied for RWGS reactions still cannot meet the characteristics of high CO2 conversion rate, high CO production rate and high CO selectivity at the same time. For example, Wang et al., reported an Au/TiO2 catalyst with a CO production rate of less than 43.2 mmol gcat −1 h−1 at 400 °C and irradiation with green light. In addition, the loading of various metals on metal oxides has been widely used in various reactions, among which platinum (Pt)-based catalysts are widely used in RWGS reactions. Therefore, in view of the above research analysis, it is a promising method to develop a catalyst for RWGS reaction by combining anatase and rutile combined with nitrogen-doped carbon and supporting Pt.

In this work, we synthesized a metal–organic framework-derived nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase TiO2 nanomaterial supported Pt nanoparticles (NPs) catalyst (Pt/TiO2@CN) for efficient photo-thermal co-catalytic RWGS reaction. Among them, the catalyst performance is the best after the support is loaded with Pt (Pt/TiO2@CN-525) calcined at 525 °C. The catalyst has a CO2 conversion rate of 42.79 %, a CO production rate of 81.46 mmol gcat −1 h−1, and a selectivity of over 99.9 % at 400 °C and 1.2W cm−2. The loading of Pt nanoparticles is beneficial to the activation and dissociation of hydrogen molecules, thereby increasing the production rate of CO. The smaller band gap width of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 is more likely to generate photoexcited electron-hole pairs, which is beneficial to the RWGS reaction. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) proved that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 is rich in oxygen defects, which is beneficial to the adsorption and activation of CO2. Finally, the mechanism of the photo-thermal co-catalyzed RWGS reaction was preliminarily discussed, and the results showed that the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 photo-thermal co-catalyzed RWGS reaction followed the COOH* mechanism.

All reagents were used without further purification. 2-aminoterephthalic acid (AR, 98 %), p-phthalic acid (AR, 99 %), tetrabutyl titanate (AR, 99 %), and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) (AR, 99.5 %) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Methanol (CH3OH) (AR, 99 %), chloroplatinic acid hexahydrate (H2PtCl6·6H2O) (AR, 99 %) were purchased from Meryer (Shanghai) Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. The deionized water was purified by pure water purifier.

NH2-MIL-125 was first synthesized via a solvothermal method. Briefly, 2-aminoterephthalic acid, tetrabutyl titanate, methanol, and DMF were charged into a Teflon-lined autoclave (100 mL). The mixed solution was stirred thoroughly and then placed at 150 °C for a heating time of 48 h. After cooling naturally to room temperature, the as-prepared powders were washed with DMF and methanol and then vacuum dried at 60 °C to obtain NH2-MIL-125. NH2-MIL-125 was calcined at a certain temperature (450, 525, 600, 675 and 750 °C) for 6 h at a heating rate of 3 °C min−1 in an N2 atmosphere, and then cooled to room temperature to obtain a TiO2@CN-x sample (x = 450, 525, 600, 675 and 750 °C). For comparison, the TiO2@C-x support was synthesized from p-phthalic acid using the same method.

Pt/TiO2@CN-x and Pt/TiO2@C-x were prepared by impregnation method. Typically, the support was dispersed in 10 mL of deionized water, and then a certain amount of H2PtCl6 solution was added. The solution was stirred well and then heated in a heater at 80 °C. The dried material was calcined under N2 atmosphere at 500 °C for a heating time of 4 h. Finally, the solid powders obtained after calcination were pressed into small particles (20 ∼ 40 mesh), and then placed in a reactor and reduced with H2 for 1 h (400 °C) to obtain Pt/TiO2@CN-x and Pt/TiO2@C-x catalysts, wherein the loading of Pt was 1.0 wt%.

The scanning electron microscope (SEM) were carried out on a Hitachi SU8230 instrument. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) were obtained on a JEM 2100F model with an operating voltage of 200 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) were analyzed to characterize the structure and crystallization. The catalysts were analyzed by XRD using a SmartLab SE diffractometer under Cu Kα radiation at 40 kV and 30 mA (scanning range 10°–80°). Raman spectra of the samples were collected from a HORIBA XploRA Raman spectrometer. The specific surface area, pore volume and average pore diameter of the samples were calculated accordingly using the Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method and the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method at a temperature of 77 K using a Quantachrome Autosorb IQ instrument. The chemical states of Pt, Ti, O, C, N were determined using a ThermoFischer ESCALAB 250Xi X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and charge corrected by adjusting C 1s to 284.8 eV. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra of the samples were obtained at room temperature using a Bruker A300-9.5/12 instrument (Germany).

H2 temperature-programmed reduction (H2-TPR), CO temperature-programmed desorption (CO-TPD), and CO2 temperature-programmed desorption (CO2-TPD) experiments were performed on a BELCAT-A chemisorption analyzer. The procedure for H2-TPR is to weigh 50–100 mg of sample in a reaction tube, ramp from room temperature to 300 °C at 10 °C min−1 for dry pretreatment, and purge with He air (30 mL min−1) for 1 h. After cooling to 50 °C, the sample is introduced into a 10 % H2/Ar mixture (30–50 mL min−1), and then ramped up to 780 °C at a ramp rate of 10 °C min−1 under the atmosphere. The procedure of CO-TPD was to weigh 50–100 mg of sample in a reaction tube, and then increase the temperature from room temperature to 300 °C at 10 °C min−1 for drying pretreatment, and then purge with He air flow (30 mL min−1) for 1 h. After cooling down to 50 °C, the sample was put into a 10 % CO/He mixture (30–50 mL min−1) for 1 h to saturation, and then switch to He air flow (30 mL min−1) for 1 h to remove the weakly physically adsorbed CO. Finally, it was desorbed under He atmosphere at a rate of 10 °C min−1 to 780 °C, and the off-gas was detected by TCD. The steps for CO2-TPD are similar to those above.

Photoluminescence (PL) spectra were collected on a Hitachi F-4600 fluorescence spectrophotometer with an excitation wavelength of 250 nm. Photocurrent, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and Mott-Schottky (M–S) were detected on a CHI 760E electrochemical workstation using a standard three-electrode system. Silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) and platinum sheets were used as reference and counter electrodes, respectively, and the working electrodes were TiO2@CN-525, Pt/TiO2@C-525 and Pt/TiO2@CN-x coated FTO glass. The sample to be tested was uniformly applied on the FTO sheet over an area of approximately 1 cm2 as the working electrode. A 0.5 M Na2SO4 solution was provided as a backup electrolyte and the light source was a 300 W Xe lamp. The photothermal conversion capacity of the samples was tested using a hand-held pyrometric thermal imaging camera (DS-2TPH10-3AUF). UV–vis diffuse reflectance spectra (UV–vis DRS) within 200–800 nm were recorded using a Shimadzu UV-2600 spectrophotometer.

In-situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) under additive light submission was tested on a Bruker INVENIO S instrument. The catalyst was heated under N2 purge to 350 °C. After stabilizing for a period of time, purge for a certain period of time and then the background spectrum was collected. Pass pure CO2 under light conditions for 60 min. Then N2 purge for a certain time and then collect the spectra of different time periods. Subsequently, the gas for the reaction was converted to 10 % H2/Ar for a certain period of time and the spectra were also collected at different time periods.

The photo-thermal co-catalytic CO2 reduction reaction was carried out in a fixed-bed quartz glass tube reactor. Typically, 0.16 g of catalyst (20 ∼ 40 mesh) and 0.52 g of silicon carbide (SiC) were mixed homogeneously and placed in the center of the tubular reactor (Fig. S1). Prior to the catalytic test, the catalyst was heated up to 400 °C under an atmosphere of 20 mL min−1 of N2. Subsequently, the catalyst was switched to an atmosphere of H2 and reduced at 400 °C for 1 h. The catalyst was then started to be evaluated for RWGS reaction performance. The gas was switched to a reaction gas mixture with CO2 and H2 as feed gas, and the ratio of CO2, H2 and internal standard gas N2 is 1:4:2. Except when evaluating the long-cycle stability test of Pt/TiO2@CN-525, the flow rate was 96 mL min−1 (gas-hour space velocity: 36,000 mL gcat −1 h−1). The flow rate of the raw gas in the remaining tests was 64 mL min−1 (gas-hour space velocity: 24,000 mL gcat −1 h−1). In addition, a 300 W Xe lamp with a power density of 1.2 W cm−2 was selected as the light source during the photo-thermal reaction. The reaction temperature was controlled by detecting the temperature of the catalyst in the reactor with a thermocouple. Catalyst testing was performed between 250 °C and 500 °C. The output gas product passes through the reactor and enters the connected Agilent GC-8860 chromatograph (equipped with a TCD detector). At the end of the reaction, the catalyst was naturally cooled to room temperature under N2 atmosphere. The CO2 conversion rate (X CO 2 , %) is calculated through the following Eq. (1), Eq. (2) is used to calculate the CO selectivity (SCO, %), and Eqs. (3) and (4) are used to calculate the CO production rate (RCO, mmol gcat −1 h−1). (1) X CO 2 = M CO 2 in - M CO 2 out M CO 2 in × 100 (2) S C O = M CO out M CO out + M CH 4 out × 100 (3) n c o = [ CO ] × F 22.4 (4) R C O = n co Weight of catalyst × 60 Where, M CO 2 in and M CO 2 out represent the CO2 content in the incoming and outgoing chromatograph, respectively. M CO out and M CH 4 out represent the CO and CH4 content in the outgoing chromatograph, respectively. F is the reaction gas flow rate (mL min−1) and [CO] is the concentration of CO (vol%) detected by the on-line gas chromatograph.

In this study, nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase TiO2 nanomaterials were synthesized by calcination pyrolysis of NH2-MIL-125 at different temperatures under N2 conditions. Platinum oxide species were then loaded on TiO2@CN support by impregnation and calcination, and finally the platinum oxide was reduced to Pt NPs by H2 reduction step. The preparation process is shown in Fig. 1 a. The surface morphological characteristics of the synthesized catalysts were preliminarily observed through SEM. The NH2-MIL-125 showed a block structure with rounded edges (Fig. S2). The SEM images in Fig. 1b–c show that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 is also a block structure with rounded edges, but its surface is rough. This is due to the decomposition of metal–organic ligands and metal ions into N-doped carbon and TiO2 during the pyrolysis process, respectively. Fig. S3 shows SEM images of Pt/TiO2@CN-450, Pt/TiO2@CN-600, Pt/TiO2@CN-675 and Pt/TiO2@CN-750. As can be seen from the figure, when the calcination temperature is too high, the catalyst surface becomes rougher and the block structure with rounded edges changes. From Fig. 1d, it is found that Pt NPs are relatively uniformly dispersed on the support, and their average size is 2.18 ± 0.55 nm. The morphology of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 was further observed by TEM and HR-TEM (Fig. 1e–f). The lattice spacing of the two TiO2 NPs was observed, with 0.33 nm corresponding to the (110) plane of rutile TiO2 and 0.35 nm to the (101) plane of anatase TiO2. The EDS elemental map also reveals the degree of dispersion of Pt, Ti, O, C and N elements, further indicating that the dispersion of Pt is relatively uniform (Fig. 1g).

The crystal structure of Pt/TiO2@CN-x at different calcination temperatures were analyzed by XRD, as shown in Fig. 2 a. It can be clearly seen that the characteristic peaks with 2θ of 25.3°, 37.8°, 48.0° and 55.07° respectively correspond to the (101), (004), (200) and (211) crystal planes of anatase TiO2 (PDF#71-1166), while the (110), (101), (111), (211) and (220) crystal planes of rutile TiO2 (PDF#86-0147) were also observed at 27.5°, 36.0°, 41.2°, 54.3° and 56.6°. It is shown that the synthesized samples consist of both anatase and rutile phases of TiO2. The XRD of Pt/TiO2@CN-675 and Pt/TiO2@CN-750 shows that the rutile diffraction peak becomes stronger and the anatase diffraction peak becomes weaker, indicating that anatase transforms into the rutile phase as the pyrolysis temperature increases. Fig. S4a shows the TEM image of Pt/TiO2@CN-750 with the average size of Pt NPs of 2.30 ± 0.35 nm, indicating that the high calcination temperature makes the average size of Pt larger. The lattice spacing of only one TiO2 phase was observed from the HR-TEM of Pt/TiO2@CN-750 as the (110) plane of rutile TiO2 (Fig. S4b). This indicates a low content of anatase, which corresponds to the XRD. The obvious peak of Pt/TiO2@C-525 in Fig. 2b belongs to anatase TiO2, which has less anatase–rutile phase. In addition, the intensity of the XRD peaks became stronger after loading Pt compared to TiO2@CN-525, which was attributed to the strengthening of its crystalline structure by twice calcination of Pt/TiO2@CN-525. No obvious Pt peak is observed in the figure, indicating that Pt has high dispersion and low content.

The crystal structure and composition of the sample were further verified by Raman spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. 2c, the peaks displayed at 148.4, 417.2, 507.9, and 617.9 cm−1 are the Eg, B1g, A1g + B1g, and A1g vibration modes of the anatase phase. The Raman peaks of rutile are located at 241.0 cm−1 and 595.8 cm−1 respectively. For Pt/TiO2@CN-675 and Pt/TiO2@CN-750 samples, the peak at 148.4 cm−1 disappears, the peak intensity at 241.0 cm−1 becomes stronger, and the peak at 617.9 cm−1 also moves toward low Raman frequency shift. These results further indicate that increasing pyrolysis temperature will transform anatase into the rutile phase, which is consistent with the XRD results. In addition, the Raman peak at 1350.0 cm−1 represents the D band of defective sites and disordered carbon in graphitized carbon, while the peak at 1590.0 cm−1 is the G band of crystalline graphitic carbon, and the results are shown in Fig. 2d.

To analyze the specific surface area and porosity of the prepared samples, N2 adsorption–desorption measurements were also performed (Fig. 2e–f and Table S1). The isotherms of all samples in the figure show type IV curves and hysteresis loops, indicating that they are mainly mesoporous structures. At the same time, the BJH pore size distribution curve in Fig. 2f observed that the sample is porous, and porosity is beneficial to the exposure of more active sites and the transport and diffusion of reactant/product molecules, thereby improving the reaction performance. Table S1 lists the BET surface area, average pore size and pore volume of TiO2@CN-525 and Pt/TiO2@CN-x. The specific surface area and pore volume of the samples unloaded with Pt were significantly smaller than that of the other samples, which was unfavorable for the diffusion of the gas molecules and the adsorption of CO2.

XPS and EPR were used to detect the electronic structure characteristics and chemical state information of the catalyst. Fig. S5 and Table S2 show the C 1s spectral data, the characteristic peak at 284.8 eV can be related to pure graphitic sp2 carbon, while the characteristic peaks at 285.97 eV and 289.52 eV are attributed to NC and/or TiC interaction and CO. N 1s XPS spectra can be divided into Pyridinic N, Pyrrolic N and Graphitic N (Fig. S6 and Table S3). For Pt/TiO2@CN-525, the peaks at 71.80 eV and 75.26 eV belong to the Pt0 peaks of Pt 4f7/2 and Pt 4f5/2, and the peaks at 72.99 eV and 76.29 eV belong to Pt 4f7/2 and Pt 4f5/2 peak of Pt2+ (Fig. 3 a and Table S4). The reason for the occurrence of Pt2+ species may be due to partial oxidation of the sample during preparation. In Pt/TiO2@C-525, the peaks of Pt0 are located at 71.82 eV and 75.30 eV, and the peaks of Pt2+ are located at 73.00 eV and 76.30 eV. Therefore, the addition of N promotes the increase in the electron cloud density of Pt, which is beneficial to the dissociation of hydrogen. Fig. 3b and Table S5 show the characteristic Ti 2p1/2 and Ti 2p3/2 peaks of Ti4+ of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 at 464.95 eV and 459.19 eV, as well as the small peaks of Ti3+ at 463.20 eV and 458.20 eV, respectively. Compared with other samples, the binding energy of Pt 4f in Pt/TiO2@CN-525 shifts toward a lower binding energy. Correspondingly, in the spectrum of Ti 2p, the binding energy of Ti 2p in Pt/TiO2@CN-525 moves to the direction of higher binding energy. The results show that a strong interaction is formed between Pt and TiO2, which promotes electron transfer between them. For O 1s (Fig. 3c and Table S6), the XPS spectra can be divided into OL (lattice oxygen), OV (oxygen vacancy) and Oa (absorbed oxygen). Compared with TiO2@CN-525 and Pt/TiO2@C-525, the OV proportion in Pt/TiO2@CN-525 increased significantly, indicating a higher oxygen vacancy concentration. Combined with the EPR results (Fig. 3d), it can be seen that compared to other catalysts, Pt/TiO2@CN-525 shows a stronger signal at g = 2.003. It further shows that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 is rich in oxygen defects. The presence of oxygen defects is more favorable for CO2 adsorption and activation. In addition, we tested the XPS at different calcination temperatures (Figs. S7–S11 and Tables S2–S6). The gradual decrease of Pyridinic N with increasing temperature could be attributed to the gradual conversion of Pyridinic N into Pyrrolic N and Graphitic N. As the temperature increases, the OV gradually increases and the OL decreases, which may be due to the increase in temperature promotes the migration of oxygen atoms in the lattice, thus forming OV. In addition, temperature different, C 1s, Pt 4f and Ti 2p show some changes.

The TiO2@CN-x was successfully prepared by calcining at different temperatures using the preliminary synthesized NH2-MIL-125 as precursor. The Pt/TiO2@CN-x catalyst was further loaded with Pt NPs on the support and finally synthesized successfully. In contrast, TiO2@CN-525 and Pt/TiO2@C-525 were chosen as control samples because of the higher performance of the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 catalyst with support at 525 °C calcination and loaded with Pt NPs. The synthesized catalysts were tested for pure thermal and photo-thermal CO2 reduction performance using a 300 W Xe lamp as a light source in the temperature interval 250 °C–500 °C. CH4 and CO were the main products of all the reactions.

Figs. S12–S14 show the CO2 conversion, CO selectivity and CO production rate of the catalysts at different calcination temperatures. The CO selectivity of all catalysts was above 99 %, but the CO2 conversion and CO production rate were lower when the calcination temperature was too high or too low. The CO2 conversion and CO production rate of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 were significantly higher than those of the samples at other calcination temperatures, which indicated that 525 °C was the optimal calcination temperature for the support. The reduction temperature significantly influences the performance of the catalyst. Consequently, we investigated the impact of various reduction temperatures on the performance of the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 catalyst in the RWGS reaction. As illustrated in Fig. S15, the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 catalyst exhibits optimal performance at a reduction temperature of 400 °C; deviations from this temperature, either higher or lower, result in diminished reaction performance. As shown in Fig. 4 a, the CO2 conversion of nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase TiO2 nanomaterials loaded with Pt catalysts under calcination conditions at 525 °C was relatively high. It is clear from the figure that the presence of Pt promoted the conversion of CO2. On the contrary, the conversion of CO2 for TiO2@CN was relatively low. The catalytic CO2 conversion of the catalysts was significantly improved with the addition of light compared with that under purely thermal conditions, indicating that the addition of light played a positive role in the conversion of CO2. The CO selectivity of Fig. 4b demonstrates that the CO selectivity of all catalysts is above 99 %. Fig. 4c tests the rate of CO production with as well as without the addition of light. Under the pure thermal condition of 400 °C, the CO production rate catalyzed by Pt/TiO2@CN-525 was 67.14 mmol gcat −1 h−1. After adding light, the production rate increased to 81.46 mmol gcat −1 h−1. Both TiO2@CN-525 and Pt/TiO2@C-525 have significantly lower production rates than Pt/TiO2@CN-525. The CO production rate of TiO2@CN-525 under photo-thermal conditions is only 3.11 mmol gcat −1 h−1. The above results indicated that the N doping and the loading of Pt could significantly improve the reaction performance of RWGS, and the light could also improve the CO2 reduction reaction. Considering the possible influence of SiC on the reaction, the effect of pure SiC on the RWGS reaction under photo-thermal conditions was evaluated (Fig. S16). The results showed that SiC exhibited very low CO2 conversion and had little effect on the reaction.

The apparent activation energies (Ea) were calculated according to the Arrhenius formula to further investigate the differences in reaction rates under different conditions (Fig. 4d and Fig. S17). Under purely thermal conditions, the Ea of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 was about 63.47 kJ mol−1, which decreased to 55.73 kJ mol−1 in the presence of light. As known from the figure, the Ea values of photo-thermal co-catalyzed reactions are smaller than those of purely thermal catalyzed reactions, indicating that light can promote the activation of reactants. In addition, the stability properties of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 were explored at 400 °C under 1.2 W cm−2 light intensity, as shown in Fig. 4e. After three dark-light cycles, the CO2 conversion was stabilized at about 34 % under dark conditions and about 39 % in the presence of light. Moreover, the selectivity has been stabilized above 99.9 %. After the stability test, no more obvious aggregation of Pt NPs was found in the TEM images, and the average size of the Pt NPs did not change much compared with those before the reaction (Fig. S18). Moreover, the XRD after the reaction also showed almost no obvious changes compared with those before the reaction (Fig. S19), which further demonstrated the superior stability of the CO2 reduction reaction catalyzed by Pt/TiO2@CN-525.

In order to further observe the catalytic performance of Pt/TiO2@CN-525, its 400 °C performance ability of the reaction was tested at different light intensities and different gas-hour space velocities (Figs. S20–S21). It can be clearly seen that the performance improves with increasing light intensity. What’s more, the CO2 conversion rate decreases but the CO production rate increases with increasing gas-hour space velocity. Furthermore, the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 performance in the present work was compared with those of the recently reported catalysts for RWGS reaction (Fig. 4f, Fig. S22 and Table S7). In the present study, Pt/TiO2@CN-525 showed considerable catalytic performance in catalyzing CO2 reduction, which is better than many catalysts currently used for RWGS reactions.

The reducing properties of the resulting samples were studied by H2-TPR (Fig. 5 a). The reduction peaks of platinum oxide species of Pt/TiO2@C-525 and Pt/TiO2@CN-525 are shown at 101.5 °C and 75.8 °C, respectively. The peaks appearing within 300–700 °C in the figure are due to reduction on the surface or inside the support. Compared with the other two catalysts, the reduction peaks in Pt/TiO2@CN-525 shift to lower temperature, indicating that the loading of Pt and the addition of N promote the reduction of platinum oxide and support, thereby producing more activity sites and oxygen vacancies to promote the RWGS reaction. CO2-TPD shows that the three samples have peaks at weakly alkaline sites, medium alkaline sites and strong alkaline sites, and all show strong CO2-TPD signals (Fig. S23). Fig. 5b shows that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 exhibits a relatively weak CO-TPD signal, which indicates that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 has a strong CO desorption ability. This result shows that it is conducive to the occurrence of further RWGS reaction, but the generation of CH4 is difficult. For example, Zhao et al., studied atomically dispersed Pt/CeO2 catalysts. They showed that the weak adsorption of CO on the catalysts inhibits excess hydrogenation and leads to a rather high CO selectivity. In contrast, the strong adsorption strength of CO leads to its further hydrogenation to CH4.

In terms of photo-electric characteristics, PL spectroscopy was first tested to assess the separation efficiency and migration efficiency of photo-generated carriers. Higher PL intensity indicates higher photo-generated carriers recombination rate. Fig. 6 a shows the PL spectra under 250 nm excitation to detect the separation and migration process of photo-generated carriers. From the figure, it is clearly seen that when the calcination temperature is too high or too low, the photo-generated carriers recombination rate is higher, showing a higher PL signal intensity. While Pt/TiO2@CN-525 has a lower PL intensity, indicating that it has a lower recombination rate of photo-generated carriers, which is very favorable for photo-thermal catalyzed CO2 reduction. In addition, TiO2@CN-525 and Pt/TiO2@C-525 also exhibited relatively high PL intensities. Fig. 6b shows the photocurrent response of the samples to further elucidate the separation and migration efficiency of the photo-generated carriers. As can be seen from the figure, when the lamp was turned on, all samples showed a photocurrent response of certain intensity. When the lamp was turned off, the photocurrent intensity decreased rapidly. Among them, Pt/TiO2@CN-525 showed the strongest photocurrent response, indicating a high photo-generated carriers separation efficiency. On the contrary, the TiO2@CN-525 exhibited the lowest photocurrent response. Furthermore, the EIS test results confirm these findings (Fig. 6c). The circular radius of TiO2@CN-525 is the largest, and the circular radius of the Pt/TiO2@CN-x samples is significantly shortened after loading Pt. Pt/TiO2@CN-525 exhibited the smallest circular radius. The absence of N as well as too high or too low calcination temperature exhibited a larger circular radius. The above results indicate that the loading of Pt, the addition of N and the appropriate calcination temperature can well reduce the recombination of photo-generated carriers.

The optical absorption properties of TiO2@CN-525, Pt/TiO2@C-525 and all Pt/TiO2@CN-x samples were investigated using UV–vis diffuse reflectance spectra (UV–vis DRS) (Fig. 6d). All catalyst samples showed significant absorption in the 200–300 nm region, which could be due to the TiO2 electrons jump from the valence band to the conduction band in the presence of light. In addition, a relatively broad absorption band was found in the 300–800 nm wavelength range, which may be due to black and carbon doping. Interestingly, there is a decreasing trend in the 330–400 nm region for Pt/TiO2@CN-675 and Pt/TiO2@CN-750. The analysis may be due to the change in the crystal structure of the samples by the high calcination temperature, which leads to a change in their optical absorption properties, which corresponds to the XRD in Fig. 2a. Fig. 6e and Figs. S24–S25 show the photo-thermal conversion capacity of the samples. All samples initially showed similar photo-thermal conversion capabilities, with a significant increase in the photo-thermal conversion capabilities of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 when the illumination time was longer than 400 s. Fig. S26 shows a Mott-Schottky plot of the sample, showing the flat band position for each catalyst. All samples show a positive slope, proving the typical of n-type semiconductors. Based on the Tauc plots (Fig. S27), the bandgap widths of TiO2@CN-525, Pt/TiO2@C-525, Pt/TiO2@CN-450, Pt/TiO2@CN-525, Pt/TiO2@CN-600, Pt/TiO2@CN-675 and Pt/TiO2@CN-750 are 1.64, 1.50, 1.59, 1.40, 1.46, 2.56 and 2.61 V, respectively. Based on the Mott-Schottky and Tauc plots, the energy band structures of the catalysts are schematically shown in Fig. 6f and Fig. S28. It is observed that Pt/TiO2@CN-525 shows the narrowest band gap width, and the smaller band gap is more likely to generate photo-excited electron-hole pairs, which promotes the photo-thermally catalyzed CO2 reduction reaction.

To investigate the causes of product generation and the RWGS reaction pathway, the intermediates on Pt/TiO2@CN-525 during photo-thermal co-catalyzed CO2 reduction were detected using in-situ DRIFTS. As shown in Fig. 7 a, the peaks observed during the reaction were CO2 (2345 cm−1) and CO3 2− (1103 cm−1, 1259 cm−1 and 1723 cm−1). A new peak attributable to COOH* (1170 cm−1) was observed after H2 pass. COOH* is usually considered as a key intermediate for the production of CO, indicating that the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 photo-thermally co-catalyzed RWGS reaction follows the COOH* mechanism.

According to the previous analytical results it was shown that the appropriate calcination temperature and the addition of N can form a dual-phase TiO2 structure. The dual-phase TiO2 can form anatase–rutile phase junction, which is favorable to reducing the possibility of photo-generated carriers recombination. The photo-electric performance test also shows that the loading of Pt, the addition of N and the appropriate calcination temperature can effectively reduce the recombination of photo-generated carriers, which is conducive to the improvement of the photo-thermal co-catalytic RWGS reaction performance. The above performance analyses indicate that the addition of N, the loading of Pt and the calcination temperature of the support at 525 °C can significantly improve the performance of the RWGS reaction. The photo-thermal co-catalyzed RWGS reaction of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 exhibits good reactivity and stability. In addition, because of the addition of N, the loading of Pt and the presence of the dual-phase structure led to a significant reduction in the reaction activation energy. Based on the results of experiments such as XPS and in-situ DRIFTS, the proposed CO2 conversion reaction pathway is shown in Fig. 7b. Pt/TiO2@CN-525 is irradiated in the full spectrum to generate electron-hole pairs, and the photo-generated electrons and holes migrate to the surface of the catalyst to participate in the CO2 reduction reaction. The reaction of H2 and holes generates H* and provides H* at a much faster rate than thermal excitation, which will further overflow to reactive CO2 adsorbed onto the OV on the support to form COOH* intermediates. Upon further activation of the CO bonds of COOH*, CO eventually dissociates from the surface, leaving the OV to continuously adsorb and activate CO2.

In summary, we developed a simple strategy to synthesize nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanomaterials by calcining NH2-MIL-125, which was preliminarily synthesized via a solvothermal method under a N2 atmosphere. Among the synthesized materials, the Pt/TiO2@CN-525 catalyst, calcined at 525 °C, showed exceptional performance in the reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction. A critical aspect of our strategy is that the incorporation of platinum (Pt) nanoparticles enhances the activation and dissociation of hydrogen molecules, thereby increasing the production rate of carbon monoxide (CO). The Pt/TiO2@CN-525 catalyst, characterized by its nitrogen-doped carbon composite dual-phase TiO2 nanomaterial, possesses abundant oxygen vacancies, which facilitate the adsorption and activation of carbon dioxide (CO2). Additionally, the presence of Pt, the introduction of nitrogen, and the optimization of calcination temperature contribute to improved light responsiveness and reduced recombination of photo-generated carriers. Notably, the catalytic performance of Pt/TiO2@CN-525 surpasses that of most RWGS catalysts reported to date, achieving commendable RWGS reaction performance. This study not only presents a valuable opportunity for the rational design of metal–organic framework (MOF)-derived composite dual-phase nanomaterials but also broadens the future application potential of Pt-based catalysts in photo-thermal catalytic CO2 reduction.
